newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Inflation fight may be hard for Hungary - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Inflation fight may be hard for Hungary - analysts.

text.p: Analysts are split over the question of whether Hungary will be able to radically slash inflation next year, which is being urged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Most analysts say if the government wants to cut inflation in 1998 quicker than the originally planned five percent, it will have to reach wide-ranging social consensus on a sharp decrease in the pace of wage and price rises next year.
"A social and economic agreement should be reached (for a substantial cut in 1998 inflation)," said Peter Bozso, analyst of OTP Securities. "But this is very difficult to carry out. "
Hungary plans to reduce inflation to 17 to 19 percent in 1997 from 23.6 percent last year, and to cut it by at least further five percentage points in 1998.

Finance Ministry officials, urged by the IMF to produce a radical cut, said recently that the 1998 budget draft, already being prepared, may include a reduction larger than five percent and may even target single-figure inflation.
The ministry said prices were already almost fully liberalised and the state of the economy did not justify high inflation, which is now running at some 19 percent year-on-year.

A drastic cut in inflation would substantially decrease the interest payments on state debt, enabling the government to cut expenditure and lower tax rates, thus boosting the economy, the ministry said.
The main stumbling block in the way of this ambitious plan is what both analysts and politicians refer to as "the psychological factor".

Hungarians have lived with high inflation rates in the past few years and, after a more than 15 percent slump in real wages in the past two years, it would be hard to convince them to risk yet another large decline in real wages, analysts said.
"People have got used to galloping wages," said Judit Barta, analyst of GKI Research Institute.
The Socialist-Liberal government was also in a difficult position if it wanted to curb wage rises ahead of the 1998 elections, analysts added.
"The prospect (of the elections) would be heavily felt during wage negotiations," said ING Barings analyst Douglas Reid.
The two ruling parties' popularity is at an all-time low and well below the total support of opposition parties, following a decline in living standards and a scandal over alleged corruption.
"I am an economist but I do not think the political background (of a price and wage agreement) is secured," said Barta.
All analysts agree that Hungary's inflation will steadily decline in the next two years and many say that the economy is ripe for low inflation.

But other analysts said that necessary and costly structural changes, such as the reform of social security, were likely to slow the decline of inflation and recreate inflationary pressures later if delayed for political reasons.
They said one key question was how quickly Hungary could cut the current 1.2 percent monthly crawling peg devaluation rate of its currency.
But as economic growth has been picking up since the second half of last year, imports and the country's trade deficit increased rapidly.
This must warn the government not to cut the devaluation rate to quickly, otherwise the growing trade gap may threaten the country's balance of payment, analysts said.
